text: After greetings, the host returns to the subject of sugar. She recalls the earlier claim that sugar is generally acceptable and asks Dr. Diaa to explain; he begins by saying table sugar is chemically sucrose.
He explains that sucrose is made of glucose and fructose and says white sugar is commonly produced from sugar beet or sugar cane.
He gives historical context about the sugar industry, including its connection to slavery in the Americas, and describes sugar as an important strategic commodity.
He continues the historical discussion, saying people used dates, raisins, and grapes as sweeteners before refined sugar became widely produced.
He describes older methods of concentrating sweetness from fruit and dates. The discussion then turns to the common phrase that sugar is a 'white poison.'
He rejects the 'white poison' label and compares refined sugar favorably with honey, referring to religious descriptions of honey as beneficial.
He says honey contains a large proportion of glucose and argues that dissolved sugar is absorbed very easily; he also mentions sugar water being used when blood sugar is low.
He questions how sugar can be described in one context as fuel for the brain and in another as a toxin, and challenges the use of the word 'poison.'
He argues that sugar is essential to life and rejects the idea that ordinary sugar intake should be compared with deliberate poisoning.
In his view, glucose is not only an energy source but also a metabolic raw material involved in glycogen storage and other biochemical processes.
He says finding high glucose during inflammation or heart problems does not prove glucose caused them, comparing this with confusing correlation and causation.
The host points out that excess can be harmful and asks whether his claim applies to all sugars, including sugar in fruit; he says he does not necessarily want the fiber.
They discuss fiber, with Dr. Diaa saying some types are easier to digest than others. The host says she wants to compare his claims with scientific studies.
He asks for the actual conclusions of studies rather than general references and challenges the statement that white sugar is toxic.
The host asks directly whether people can eat as much sugar as they want without becoming ill. He answers yes, prompting her to ask how that could be true.
Dr. Diaa says he rejects the usual framing of 'diabetes disease' and asks whether lowering glucose alone would reverse all of a patient's other symptoms.
He questions the conventional categories of diabetes and lists several types, arguing that the classifications do not fully explain the underlying cause.
He says symptoms can precede high glucose and may remain after glucose is lowered, and he asks to return to first principles and define diabetes.
They discuss the standard definition of diabetes as abnormal glucose regulation, and he questions whether insulin deficiency, insulin resistance, or cell damage is the true cause.
He argues that if high glucose itself caused damage, it would not explain years of earlier symptoms such as tremor, nerve complaints, sexual problems, and gastrointestinal symptoms.
He challenges the idea of calling changing medical interpretations 'facts' and asks whether the real reason for high glucose is actually known.
He criticizes research that, in his view, often ends with a new glucose-lowering drug rather than a cure, and introduces his alternative explanation.
He says the body can intentionally raise glucose during stress, illness, pain, diarrhea, or toxin exposure through cortisol and adrenaline.
He gives strenuous exercise and fasting as examples where glucose can rise without eating, saying the body increases production to support the brain and nervous system.
He extends this argument to cell replacement and metabolism, then attributes some dizziness episodes to digestive problems and abdominal distension.
The host asks whether he means the colon; he says he means the digestive tract more broadly and gives poisoning as an example of a stress response.
He argues that emergency stress hormones such as adrenaline and corticosteroids raise glucose and that insulin is not the main emergency hormone in those situations.
He says the liver can make glucose from substances such as lactate, pyruvate, amino acids, and other metabolic substrates; the host then asks about diabetic coma.
He claims coma is fundamentally related to inadequate brain perfusion and discusses different labels for diabetic coma, then says unexplained low glucose points to liver dysfunction.
He shifts attention from the pancreas to the liver and describes the pancreas mainly as a digestive gland, while a smaller endocrine portion produces insulin and glucagon.
He says insulin and glucagon enter the portal circulation and claims much of the insulin is cleared by the liver before reaching the rest of the body.
He concludes that only a fraction reaches peripheral tissues and argues that systemic insulin can cause hypoglycemia; the host asks him to slow down and continue carefully.
The host asks whether his dietary approach has successfully treated people with diabetes. He questions why he was invited, and she says the program presents different medical schools of thought.
He says he is already known for controversial views and states clearly his claim that high blood sugar itself is not harmful.
He says a very high glucose reading may instead reflect physiological stress and claims the body may need glucose rather than insulin during infections or inflammation.
The host brings endocrinologist Dr. Omar El-Saadany onto the phone. He says the claims conflict with American, European, Canadian, and Egyptian diabetes guidelines.
Dr. Omar says vascular, nerve, and eye complications can begin early and argues that high glucose in illness or surgery may need treatment rather than more sugar.
He asks for references supporting Dr. Diaa's claims and says they conflict with established standards of care.
Dr. Diaa responds that a 'guideline' is guidance rather than an absolute rule and says he has consciously departed from the conventional approach.
Dr. Omar says international guidelines cannot simply be dismissed. Dr. Diaa challenges him about his practical experience, and Dr. Omar cites decades of specialist work.
The host redirects the discussion from credentials back to science. Dr. Omar explains that prediabetes may exist for years before overt diabetes appears.
He says macrovascular complications can begin years earlier and that pancreatic beta-cell function may already be substantially reduced by the time diabetes is diagnosed.
Dr. Omar stresses evidence levels and large studies, then the discussion turns to whether diabetes can be treated without insulin.
He says type 1 diabetes requires insulin, while a temporary 'honeymoon' period may allow lower doses early on.
He adds that treatment decisions should follow evidence and complication risk, including cardiovascular and microvascular outcomes.
Dr. Diaa returns to his question: if damage develops during years when glucose is not yet high, why should glucose itself be blamed?
The exchange becomes tense over prediabetes, with Dr. Diaa insisting that his question concerns damage occurring before glucose rises.
They challenge each other's qualifications and tone, and the discussion shifts from the scientific point to who should debate whom and in what setting.
Dr. Omar asks to end the call because of the tone. The host thanks him and tries to calm the exchange while emphasizing respect for both doctors.
The host says the goal is not a fight but to give viewers useful information and allow competing viewpoints to be heard.
She notes that technical terms such as 'evidence-based' may not be clear to viewers and asks Dr. Omar for a simple explanation of diabetes treatment.
Dr. Omar says treatment depends on the type: type 1 requires insulin; type 2 generally starts with lifestyle measures and commonly used medications, then treatment is adjusted for risk.
He says that by diagnosis, pancreatic beta-cell function may already be reduced, so treatment aims to preserve remaining function rather than add more sugar.
The conversation again becomes personal, with requests to state titles, experience, and evidence rather than argue about status.
Dr. Omar objects strongly to the idea of giving more sugar to someone with high glucose, while Dr. Diaa argues that sugar would be used only in hypoglycemia; the tone deteriorates.
Dr. Omar asks the host to verify guests' credentials and says he will complain to broadcasting management. The host thanks him and ends the call.
The host reiterates that media should present different schools of thought and let viewers hear the range of opinions being discussed.
She asks Dr. Diaa to respond to what was said, while also trying to move past the personal confrontation and return to the ideas.
Dr. Diaa asks why damage is said to occur during years of prediabetes when glucose may not yet be frankly elevated, and the host asks him to explain simply.
He lists symptoms he says can occur during those years even while glucose remains normal and asks how that fits with the standard explanation.
He continues arguing that the pancreas may be deteriorating while glucose remains controlled, and says this leaves unanswered questions in his view.
The host says time is running short and asks one final direct question: has his approach treated people successfully?
Dr. Diaa claims roughly 3,000 people have improved or been treated using his approach, including without insulin in some cases.
He says he considers those real-world cases evidence and claims the approach can be repeated in new patients, while the host asks why it has not been formally validated.
He says he presented his ideas to specialists but believes they were rejected, and he suggests the main beneficiary would be the patient if his approach were adopted.
He argues that patients would need fewer prescriptions and follow-up visits; the host questions whether medical follow-up still has value.

He says he wants people to become less dependent on doctors and rejects routine checkups as a way to 'catch' disease early. He frames illness and death philosophically as part of life and rejects what he sees as excessive medicalization.
The discussion turns to whether refined sugar is manufactured or extracted; he argues that it is extracted from natural sources rather than invented.
The host raises processing and additives, then asks why he rejects foods such as oats or wheat while defending refined sugar; he cites genetic modification concerns.
He also argues against many vegetables and high-fiber foods, while allowing some soft fruits if they are free from pesticide contamination.
As time runs out, the host suggests a future episode with another doctor present. Dr. Diaa says he does not want to return only to hear the same guideline-based arguments.
The exchange becomes heated again. He says he has broken with the mainstream and accuses the program of seeking controversy, while the host asks him to calm down.
He says he wants an Egyptian scientist who can defend the guidelines directly; he presents himself as a doctor with his own concept and clinical experience.
The host says they tried to arrange broader discussion. They then take a call from Magued in France, who says he has been following the program.
Magued says he wants to move beyond the sugar issue and asks whether the program's goal is to create controversy. The host strongly denies that.
Magued says the program still carries responsibility because viewers may select only the claims they like and could be harmed if those claims are wrong.
He says Dr. Diaa's message may sound attractive because it simplifies things, but scientific responsibility matters when millions may be watching.
Magued adds a separate concern about smoking, saying he heard a video implying that a non-smoker is somehow less masculine, and he agrees with Dr. Omar's call for more scrutiny.
The host thanks him and says the program's role is to present different viewpoints and discuss them neutrally using scientific information.
She asks Dr. Diaa about the smoking comment. He says it came from an informal live session with his audience and should not be treated as a formal quotation.
He says he smokes and personally claims cigarettes are not harmful, then compares that stance with his broader habit of questioning accepted claims.
He says he simply used his own reasoning and deliberately broke with mainstream thinking; the host notes that his popularity has nevertheless grown.
He says he is not a media personality but someone focused on real-world results and again challenges critics to examine his record before judging him.
The host closes by saying the discussion concerns an idea that has caused significant controversy within the medical community.
